transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Well, I came in because... I just can't seem to stop my mind once it gets going. Once a worry starts—like about my mother getting up at night, or this big grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I just can't seem to shelve it in my mind. 

Speaking of the grant report, it's actually for our new digital media collection at the library, and it has been a complete nightmare to catalog. The software the university bought is just terribly outdated. I told the board we needed the newer system, but they wouldn't listen, and now I'm the one spending my weekends trying to migrate all this metadata. I even tried explaining it to my sister on Sunday, but she was too busy talking about her new kitchen remodel. They're doing this awful seafoam green tile for the backsplash, which just completely clashes with her oak cabinets, but I didn't have the heart to tell her... 

Um, but anyway, where was I? Right. I just can't put the thoughts away. No matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself, the worries just stay stuck right there in the front of my head.
Do you ever have thoughts that come into your mind that you find disturbing or unwanted, that you wish you could stop thinking about?

Disturbing or unwanted thoughts... I mean, I don't think so? Not like anything really weird or scary, if that's what you mean. Just the usual worries that I can't turn off. Like the grant report, or my mom... 

Speaking of my mom, she actually called me three times yesterday while I was trying to sort out that metadata issue I mentioned. She couldn't figure out how to reset the clock on her microwave. It's one of those over-the-range ones, you know? And honestly, the buttons are so small, I can hardly read them myself, let alone someone with her eyesight. I told her I'd come over and fix it after work, but by the time I got there, she had somehow managed to change the language on her TV to Spanish instead. We spent an hour just trying to find the settings menu... 

But, um, no. To answer your question, no disturbing thoughts. Just the regular stuff that won't leave me alone.
Do you ever feel physically restless, like you can't sit still or relax your body, even when you're not actively worrying about something?

Physically restless? No, I don't think so. I mean, I sit at a desk most of the day, so I'm pretty stationary. 

Though, getting a good chair for that desk was a whole ordeal. The university has this approved vendor list, and you can't just go buy a normal ergonomic chair from an office supply store. You have to order it through their specific catalog, and everything in there looks like it was designed in the 1990s. I finally picked one out that looked decent, but when it arrived, the lumbar support was practically non-existent. I ended up having to bring in a little throw pillow from home—the one my aunt knitted for me a few Christmases ago. It's this bright mustard yellow color, which completely clashes with the drab grey cubicle walls, but honestly, at this point, I don't even care. 

But, um, yeah, I'm not really restless or anything. I can sit still just fine.
Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels lately, like feeling more tired than usual or struggling to get through the day?

Energy levels? Um, no, I don't think I've noticed anything different. I mean, I'm tired, but who isn't, right? 

Speaking of being tired, you should see the new student assistants we got at the library this semester. They always look like they've just rolled out of bed. One of them, I think his name is Tyler, showed up on Tuesday wearing pajama pants. Literal flannel pajama pants with little cartoon penguins on them. I didn't even know what to say. When I was in library science school, we had a strict dress code for our practicums. You wouldn't dare show up in anything less than business casual. I remember I had this one navy blue blazer that I wore to almost every shift, and it had these terrible shoulder pads that I eventually had to cut out myself because I couldn't afford a tailor... 

But, um, anyway. No, my energy is fine. Just the normal amount of tired, I guess.
Have you felt down, sad, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, even for a little while, in the past couple of weeks?

Down or sad? Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't feel depressed or anything like that. I still like doing my usual stuff. 

Actually, I was just trying to organize my cross-stitch supplies this weekend. I've been working on this big floral pattern for my sister's birthday, which is coming up in November. But the embroidery floss... it's a nightmare to keep sorted. I bought one of those plastic organizers with the little compartments, you know? But the bobbins they give you to wind the thread around are so flimsy. Half of them bent before I even got the thread on them. I ended up having to order a different brand online, and of course, they got delivered to the wrong apartment. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson—he's this older gentleman on the first floor who always leaves his recycling bin out for days—he actually brought the package up to me, but the box was completely crushed on one corner... 

But, um, anyway. No, I haven't lost interest in things. I'm just as interested in my hobbies as always.
Do you ever find yourself getting irritated or frustrated because you can’t stop worrying about these things?

Irritated? Um, well, no, I don't think the worrying itself makes me frustrated. I mean, I worry, but I don't get mad about it. 

Though, speaking of being irritated, the new self-checkout kiosks they installed at the library are driving me absolutely up the wall. They're supposed to make things faster, but the barcode scanner is so finicky. If the book jacket is even slightly glossy, the laser just reflects right off it and beeps this horrible, high-pitched error noise. And then the patrons get frustrated and start tapping the screen harder and harder, like that's going to help. I had to intervene yesterday with this woman who was trying to check out a stack of cookbooks. She had this massive pile of them—mostly baking ones, which made me think about how I haven't made my grandmother's zucchini bread in ages. You really need fresh zucchini for it, not the stuff from the supermarket that's been sitting in a truck for a week. My grandmother used to grow her own in this little patch behind her garage... 

But, um, sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, the worrying doesn't really make me angry or anything.
Do you find it difficult to control your worrying, even when you know the things you’re worrying about might not be as big of a deal as they seem in your mind?

Difficult to control? Yeah, actually, that's... that's kind of why I came in. It's like, once a worry starts, I just can't seem to shelve it in my mind. No matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself, it just stays there. Like worrying about my mother getting up in the middle of the night, or this grant report I have due, or if I missed something important at work... 

Speaking of missing things at work, we had this massive inventory audit last month, and they brought in this outside consulting firm to oversee it. The lead consultant, I think her name was Brenda, wore the most overpowering floral perfume. It smelled exactly like the potpourri my great-aunt used to keep in her guest bathroom. You know, the kind with the dried rose petals and those weird little wooden balls? My great-aunt had this beautiful Victorian house with a wraparound porch, and we used to sit out there in the summers drinking iced tea. But she always put way too much sugar in it. It was practically syrup. I tried making iced tea at home last week, but I used this new loose-leaf Earl Grey I found at the farmer's market, and I think I steeped it too long because it came out incredibly bitter...

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, the worrying. Yeah, it's just really hard to turn it off once it gets going, even when I know I'm probably overthinking it.
Do you ever notice any physical symptoms like muscle tension, headaches, or stomach upset when you're worrying a lot?

Physical symptoms? Um, well, my stomach is usually fine, but... yeah, my muscles definitely get tight. By the end of the day, my neck and shoulders feel completely locked up, like I've been bracing myself for something. And I catch myself clenching my jaw a lot, especially when I'm answering emails or just sitting there listening for my mother in the next room. 

Speaking of emails, the new email system they rolled out at the library is a complete disaster. They switched us over to this cloud-based client over the weekend, and half of my folders didn't migrate properly. I had this one folder specifically for interlibrary loan requests from the historical society, and it just vanished. The historical society is actually doing this fascinating exhibit right now on local architecture from the 1920s. They have all these original blueprints from when the downtown theater was built. I went to a movie at that theater once, years ago, before they restored it. The seats were covered in this awful, scratchy red velvet, and the floor was so sticky... I think I ruined a pair of suede boots that night. They were these beautiful camel-colored boots I bought on sale... 

But, um, anyway. Yes, I do get a lot of muscle tension. My neck and shoulders just get so stiff from all the worrying.
Does the muscle tension in your neck and shoulders happen all the time, or does it get worse specifically when you're worrying more than usual?

Um, the muscle tension? I'm not really sure if it happens all the time or just when I'm worrying more. I haven't really tracked it like that. I just know my neck and shoulders are always so stiff. 

Actually, speaking of stiff, I bought this new ergonomic chair for my home office because I thought maybe it was my posture. It was supposed to have all this lumbar support, but the mesh back is so rigid it feels like leaning against a chain-link fence. I got it from that office supply store out on Route 9, the one that used to be a roller rink in the eighties. We used to go there every Friday night when I was in middle school. They played the best music—lots of synth-pop and early Madonna. I had this neon pink scrunchie I wore every single time, and I thought I looked so cool. My best friend Sarah had matching neon green shoelaces. I wonder what happened to Sarah? I think she moved to Oregon or somewhere out West to study forestry... 

But, sorry, what were you asking? Oh, if the tension gets worse when I worry. Yeah, I don't really know. I just haven't paid that close attention to the timing of it.
Is your worry something that happens to you almost every day, or does it come and go in waves where there are days when you don’t worry much at all?

Almost every day? Yeah, I'd say it's pretty much a daily thing. It feels like over this past year, it's just snowballed. It used to be mostly about my mother's safety, you know, with her living with me and all. But now my worrying has spread to everything—finances, staff decisions at the library, deadlines, the house... even just whether I’m being a good daughter. It's like even small things can start to feel like they’re about to unravel. 

Speaking of unraveling, I was trying to fix this old quilt my grandmother made. It's this beautiful double wedding ring pattern, all these pastel scraps from dresses she made in the fifties. Anyway, one of the seams started coming apart, and I thought I could just stitch it up quickly. But I couldn't find my good sewing scissors. I have this pair of Gingher shears I bought when I thought I was going to take up dressmaking. I took exactly one class at the community center. The instructor was this woman named Beatrice who had the most perfectly coiffed silver hair. It never moved, not an inch, even when she was bending over the cutting tables. She told me I had a "heavy hand" with the rotary cutter, which I think was her polite way of saying I was ruining the fabric. I ended up making this terrible A-line skirt that was completely lopsided...

Oh, I'm sorry, I drifted off again. But yes, the worrying is definitely an everyday thing now. It just touches everything.

patient.answer:
Almost every day? Yeah, I'd say it's pretty much a daily thing. It feels like over this past year, it's just snowballed. It used to be mostly about my mother's safety, you know, with her living with me and all. But now my worrying has spread to everything—finances, staff decisions at the library, deadlines, the house... even just whether I’m being a good daughter. It's like even small things can start to feel like they’re about to unravel. 

Speaking of unraveling, I was trying to fix this old quilt my grandmother made. It's this beautiful double wedding ring pattern, all these pastel scraps from dresses she made in the fifties. Anyway, one of the seams started coming apart, and I thought I could just stitch it up quickly. But I couldn't find my good sewing scissors. I have this pair of Gingher shears I bought when I thought I was going to take up dressmaking. I took exactly one class at the community center. The instructor was this woman named Beatrice who had the most perfectly coiffed silver hair. It never moved, not an inch, even when she was bending over the cutting tables. She told me I had a "heavy hand" with the rotary cutter, which I think was her polite way of saying I was ruining the fabric. I ended up making this terrible A-line skirt that was completely lopsided...

Oh, I'm sorry, I drifted off again. But yes, the worrying is definitely an everyday thing now. It just touches everything.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of persistent, excessive, and uncontrollable worry across multiple domains of life, along with associated physical symptoms (muscle tension), occurring nearly every day and causing clinically significant distress, align with a diagnosis of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1). No features of Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22) alone are sufficient to explain the chronicity and pervasiveness of symptoms, effectively ruling it out.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with excessive worry about multiple domains occurring more days than not over the past year, difficulty controlling the worry, and associated muscle tension, consistent with generalized anxiety disorder. No evidence of panic attacks, depression, or adjustment stressors that would support alternative diagnoses.
